questions.stem: Under the Canton system (1757–1842), how was European trade with China controlled?
options: Only Dutch ships were allowed into Chinese waters, on one small island
China sent its own merchant fleets to sell its goods in European ports
Foreigners could trade only at Canton, through licensed Chinese merchants
Europeans could trade freely at any Chinese port, paying no customs duties
questions.explanation: The Qing limited Western merchants to Canton (Guangzhou), where they had to deal through the licensed Cohong merchants and obey strict rules. Restricting the Dutch to one island describes Dejima, Japan's trading post at Nagasaki. British frustration with these limits was one cause of the Opium Wars.

questions.stem: Why did British merchants ship large amounts of opium from India into China in the early 1800s?
options: To trade for opium grown on farms around Canton
Because opium was legal in China but banned in India
To pay for Chinese tea without sending Britain's silver
Because the Qing emperor had officially asked Britain to supply it
questions.explanation: Britain bought huge amounts of tea, silk and porcelain but China wanted few British goods, so silver flowed to China. Selling opium grown in British India reversed the flow, even though the Qing had banned the drug. When Commissioner Lin Zexu destroyed British opium stocks in 1839, Britain went to war.

questions.stem: The Treaty of Nanjing (Nanking), which ended the First Opium War in 1842, gave Britain:
options: Macau, taken by force from the Portuguese
a promise that China would ban all opium imports
Hong Kong Island and five ports open to trade
control of Beijing and the right to name the emperor
questions.explanation: China ceded Hong Kong Island, opened five treaty ports including Shanghai and Canton, and paid a large indemnity. Macau was a Portuguese settlement and stayed so. The treaty did not even mention opium, and the trade continued.

questions.stem: Under the 'unequal treaties' forced on China in the 1800s, 'extraterritoriality' meant that:
options: China could set any tax it liked on all goods brought in by foreign merchants
foreign troops had to leave Chinese soil within one year
foreigners accused of crimes in China were tried by their own consuls
Chinese citizens could live in Britain without needing permission
questions.explanation: Extraterritoriality placed foreigners outside Chinese law, one of the reasons the treaties were seen as humiliating. The treaties also fixed low tariffs, so China could not set its own taxes on foreign goods. They are called 'unequal' because China gained nothing in return for these privileges.

questions.stem: The Taiping Rebellion (1850–64) was:
options: the revolution that ended the Qing dynasty and created a republic
a huge civil war against the Qing led by a man who claimed to be Jesus's brother
an anti-foreign uprising by secret societies that besieged the foreign embassies in Beijing
a Japanese invasion of northern China that seized Korea and Taiwan
questions.explanation: Hong Xiuquan, inspired by Christian writings, founded the Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace, and the war that followed was one of the deadliest in history. The siege of the foreign embassies was the Boxer Rebellion of 1900, and the dynasty ended with the 1911 revolution.

questions.stem: What was the aim of China's Self-Strengthening Movement (about 1861–95)?
options: Close China completely to every foreign trader and missionary
Ask Japan to take over China's army and navy
Adopt Western weapons and industry while keeping Confucian rule
Replace the emperor with a national parliament elected by all adult men
questions.explanation: Officials built arsenals, shipyards and factories to copy Western technology, but kept the traditional political system. Defeat by Japan in 1894–95 showed the reforms had not gone far enough. Opposition at court, including from the Empress Dowager Cixi, limited deeper change.

questions.stem: During the Boxer Rebellion (1899–1901):
options: anti-foreign rebels besieged Beijing's foreign legations until foreign troops arrived
Chinese revolutionaries overthrew the last emperor and declared a republic
British forces captured Hong Kong Island during the First Opium War
Japan defeated China's fleet at sea and forced it to give up the island of Taiwan for good
questions.explanation: The Boxers attacked foreigners and Chinese Christians, and the Qing court under Cixi backed them; an eight-nation force relieved the siege in 1900. The Australian colonies also took part, sending naval contingents from New South Wales and Victoria and South Australia's gunboat Protector. China was forced to pay a huge indemnity, weakening the Qing further.

questions.stem: Who is regarded as the founding father of the Republic of China after the 1911 revolution?
options: Puyi
Sun Yat-sen
Empress Dowager Cixi
Mao Zedong
questions.explanation: Sun Yat-sen's revolutionary movement helped bring down the Qing, and he became the first provisional president in 1912. Puyi was the boy emperor who abdicated, and Cixi had died in 1908. Mao Zedong founded the People's Republic of China much later, in 1949.

questions.stem: Which Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife?
options: Akbar
Babur
Aurangzeb
Shah Jahan
questions.explanation: Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal at Agra in the 1600s for Mumtaz Mahal. Babur founded the Mughal Empire in 1526, Akbar was famous for religious tolerance and strong government, and Aurangzeb expanded the empire before it declined in the 1700s.

questions.stem: Why is the Battle of Plassey in 1757 seen as a turning point in Indian history?
options: It began the Mughal Empire under its first emperor, Babur
It was the opening battle of the 1857 Rebellion
It gave the East India Company control of Bengal
It ended British rule in India and freed Bengal
questions.explanation: Robert Clive's victory over the Nawab of Bengal gave the Company Bengal's huge revenues, which it used to expand its power across India. The Mughal Empire had begun in 1526, and British rule lasted until 1947. Plassey was a century before the 1857 Rebellion.

questions.stem: How did the British East India Company come to control much of India by the mid-1800s?
options: Winning a single short war against all the Indian states in 1757
Being invited by a vote of the Indian princes to govern them
Using its own armies and deals with Indian rulers over about a century
Buying the whole of India outright from the Mughal emperor in a single treaty
questions.explanation: The Company, a trading business with its own army of mainly Indian soldiers called sepoys, expanded through wars, alliances and taking over states whose rulers died without heirs. Plassey in 1757 was an important start, but conquest continued into the 1850s.

questions.stem: Which grievance helped spark the Indian Rebellion of 1857 among the sepoys?
options: A ban on Indians joining the East India Company's army
Rumours that new cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat
The Company's refusal to let sepoys serve outside India
A British plan to hand power back to the Mughal emperor
questions.explanation: Soldiers had to bite the new rifle cartridges, and the grease rumour offended both Hindus and Muslims; it came on top of anger at Company annexations, land taxes and fears of forced conversion. Sepoys were in fact required to serve overseas under a recent law, which was another grievance.

questions.stem: What was the main result of the 1857 Rebellion for how India was governed?
options: The British Crown took over rule of India from the East India Company
India became independent under the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah II
The East India Company was given more soldiers and greater powers
India was divided into the separate nations of India and Pakistan
questions.explanation: After the rebellion was crushed, the Government of India Act 1858 abolished Company rule and began the British Raj, run by a viceroy for the Crown. The last Mughal emperor was exiled to Burma, and Partition came much later, with independence in 1947.

questions.stem: The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, began as:
options: an armed movement fighting to drive the British out of India
a British body set up to manage India's railways and ports
a party demanding a separate state for India's Muslims
a meeting of educated Indians seeking a greater say in government
questions.explanation: Early leaders such as Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale worked through petitions and debate, while Bal Gangadhar Tilak later pressed for more forceful demands for self-rule. Mass non-violent campaigns came under Gandhi after World War I. The All-India Muslim League was founded separately in 1906.

questions.stem: Before 1853, how did Tokugawa Japan limit contact with Europeans?
options: Dutch traders were the only Europeans allowed, confined to Dejima
British merchants alone were permitted to trade, at the city of Edo
Portuguese missionaries controlled all of Japan's foreign trade
Japan had no contact of any kind with any foreign country
questions.explanation: From the 1630s the shoguns expelled the Portuguese, banned Christianity and restricted the Dutch to the tiny artificial island of Dejima at Nagasaki. Japan still traded with China and Korea, so it was never completely cut off. This policy is often called sakoku.

questions.stem: In 1853–54 US Commodore Matthew Perry arrived in Japan with warships. What did this lead to?
options: The founding of an American colony on the island of Honshu
The Meiji emperor being removed from power by the US
The Treaty of Kanagawa, opening ports to American ships
Japan closing its ports to foreigners for the first time
questions.explanation: Faced with modern warships, the shogunate signed the Treaty of Kanagawa in 1854, ending more than two centuries of strict seclusion; unequal trade treaties followed. Japan's closure dated from the 1630s, and the humiliation helped bring down the shogunate in 1868.

questions.stem: After the Meiji Restoration of 1868, how did Japan's leaders respond to Western power?
options: They rapidly modernised the army, industry, schools and government
They returned power to the Tokugawa shoguns and closed the ports
They asked Britain to rule Japan as a protectorate for a time
They banned all Western technology and foreign learning
questions.explanation: Under the slogan 'rich country, strong army', Japan built railways, factories, a conscript army and a modern navy, introduced compulsory schooling and adopted a constitution in 1889. The Restoration ended the Tokugawa shogunate, and opponents such as the Satsuma rebels of 1877 were defeated.

questions.stem: Which war, fought in 1894–95, showed Japan's growing power and gave it Taiwan?
options: The Russo-Japanese War
The Second Opium War
The Boxer Rebellion
The First Sino-Japanese War
questions.explanation: Japan's modern forces defeated China, mainly over influence in Korea, and in the peace treaty Japan gained Taiwan. The Russo-Japanese War followed in 1904–05, and Japan annexed Korea in 1910.

questions.stem: Why did Japan's victory in the Russo-Japanese War (1904–05) shock the world?
options: Japan had never fought a war against any other country before
Japan had won the war without using any navy at all
Russia had been Britain's closest ally in Asia at the time
An Asian nation had defeated a major European power in a modern war
questions.explanation: Japan destroyed the Russian fleet at Tsushima and won control of Korea and southern Manchuria, inspiring nationalists across Asia. Its navy was central to the victory, and Britain was allied with Japan, not Russia, from 1902.

questions.stem: Japan joined World War I on the Allied side in 1914. What did it gain in Asia and the Pacific?
options: Britain's colony of Hong Kong and the busy treaty port of Shanghai
Control of the whole of mainland China and its government
Germany's islands north of the equator and its base at Tsingtao
German New Guinea and the phosphate island of Nauru
questions.explanation: Japan seized Germany's leased territory at Tsingtao (Qingdao) and its Pacific islands north of the equator, and in 1915 pressed the Twenty-One Demands on China. German New Guinea and Nauru, south of the equator, were taken by Australian forces, which is the usual mix-up.

questions.stem: Prince Diponegoro led the Java War (1825–30) against:
options: British rule in Malaya
Portuguese traders in Macau
the Japanese occupation of Java
Dutch colonial rule in Java
questions.explanation: Diponegoro, a Javanese prince, led a long guerrilla war against Dutch control; he was captured during negotiations in 1830 and exiled. He is now honoured as an Indonesian national hero. The Japanese occupation of the Dutch East Indies came much later, in World War II.

questions.stem: Under the Dutch Cultivation System (cultuurstelsel) introduced in Java in 1830, villagers had to:
options: set aside land or labour to grow export crops for the government
pay all of their taxes in Dutch silver coins shipped from Europe
grow only rice, and sell all of it to Dutch merchants in Batavia
travel to the Netherlands to work in its textile factories for several years
questions.explanation: Villages had to give part of their land, often about a fifth, or a set amount of labour to crops such as coffee, sugar and indigo, which the government sold in Europe at great profit. Rice growing suffered, and famines struck parts of Java in the 1840s. Criticism in the Netherlands later led to the 'Ethical Policy' of around 1900.

questions.stem: Budi Utomo, founded in 1908, and Sarekat Islam, founded a few years later, are significant in Indonesian history because they:
options: led the Java War against the Dutch from 1825 to 1830
declared Indonesia's full independence from the Netherlands in 1918
were early organisations of the Indonesian national awakening
were Dutch trading companies that replaced the old VOC
questions.explanation: Budi Utomo, begun by Javanese medical students, and the mass movement Sarekat Islam built a new sense of shared identity and political demands under Dutch rule. The VOC had been dissolved in 1799, and independence was declared by Sukarno and Hatta in 1945.
